'''''Sagittaria latifolia''''' is a [[wetland]] plant in the family [[Alismataceae]], native to North America and northern South America; common names include '''broadleaf arrowhead''',<ref>{{PLANTS|id=SALA2|taxon=Sagittaria latifolia|accessdate=26 October 2015}}</ref> '''duck-potato''',<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17}}</ref> '''Indian potato''', or '''wapato'''. This plant produces [[Eating|edible]] [[tuber]]s that have traditionally been extensively used by [[indigenous peoples of the Americas|Native Americans]].

==Description==
''Sagittaria latifolia'' is a variably sized [[perennial]] that may reach as much as {{Convert|150|cm|ft|sp=us|frac=2}} in height,<ref name="4Corners">{{cite book |last1=Heil |first1=Kenneth D. |last2=O'Kane, Jr. |first2=Steve L. |last3=Reeves |first3=Linda Mary |last4=Clifford |first4=Arnold |title=Flora of the Four Corners Region: Vascular Plants of the San Juan River Drainage, Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico, and Utah |date=2013 |publisher=Missouri Botanical Garden |location=St. Louis, Missouri |page=106 |url=https://archive.org/details/mobot31753003888887/page/106 |access-date=2 June 2024}}</ref> but is more typically {{Convert|60–120|cm|in|abbr=on|0}}.<ref name="NA Edible">{{cite book |last1=Elias |first1=Thomas S. |last2=Dykeman |first2=Peter A. |title=Field Guide to North American Edible Wild Plants |date=1982 |publisher=Outdoor Life Books |location=New York |isbn=978-0-442-22200-0 |page=213 |url=https://archive.org/details/fieldguidetonort0000elia/page/213 |access-date=2 June 2024 |language=en}}</ref> The plants often grow together in crowded colonies and spread by runners ([[stolon]]s) at or just under the soil surface. In late summer the plants produce [[tuber]]s that are twice as long as wide,<ref>{{cite book |last1=Runkel |first1=Sylvan T. |title=Wildflowers and Other Plants of Iowa Wetlands |date=1999 |publisher=Iowa State University Press |location=Ames, Iowa |isbn=978-0-8138-2174-0 |pages=306–307 |url=https://archive.org/details/wildflowersother0000runk/page/306 |access-date=2 June 2024}}</ref> each typically measuring {{Convert|0.5|to|5|cm|abbr=on|frac=4|in}} in diameter.<ref name="NA Edible" /> 

The plant produces [[Rosette (botany)|rosettes]] of [[leaves]] and an [[inflorescence]] on a long rigid [[Scape (botany)|scape]]. The leaves are extremely variable, from {{Convert|10-50|cm|abbr=on|frac=2}} in length<ref name="Audubon2001">{{Cite book |last=Spellenberg |first=Richard |url=https://archive.org/details/nationalaudubons00spel/page/335/ |title=National Audubon Society Field Guide to North American Wildflowers: Western Region |publisher=Knopf |year=2001 |isbn=978-0-375-40233-3 |edition=rev |page=335 |orig-date=1979}}</ref> and {{Convert|1 to 2|cm|abbr=on|frac=4}} thin to wedge-shaped like those of ''[[Sagittaria cuneata|S. cuneata]]''. Spongy and solid, the leaves have [[Parallel (geometry)|parallel]] [[Leaf#Venation (arrangement of the veins)|venation]] meeting in the middle and the extremities. The inflorescence is a [[raceme]] about {{Convert|90|cm|abbr=on}} above water and composed of white flowers [[Whorl (botany)|whorled]] by threes, blooming from July to September.<ref name="Audubon2001" /> The flowers are about {{Convert|2-4|cm|abbr=on|frac=4}} wide<ref name="Audubon2001" /> and usually divided into female on the lower part and male on the upper of the plant, although some specimens are [[dioecious]]. The flowers have three round, white [[petal]]s and three very short curved, dark green [[sepal]]s. Flower sex is easy to determine due to the dissimilarity between the 25 to 50 yellow [[stamen]]s of the male and the sphere of green [[carpel]]s (sometimes over a thousand) of the female ones.<ref>CONABIO. 2009. ==Distribution and habitat==
[[File:Sagittaria latifolia 027.jpg|thumb|left|alt=photo|''Sagittaria latifolia'', [[Sainte-Anne-de-la-Pérade]], [[Quebec]], [[Canada]] ]]
''Sagittaria latifolia'' is native to southern Canada and most of the contiguous United States, as well as [[Mexico]], [[Central America]], [[Colombia]], [[Venezuela]], [[Ecuador]], and [[Cuba]]. It is also naturalized in [[Hawaii]], [[Puerto Rico]], [[Bhutan]], [[Australia]] and much of Europe ([[France]], [[Spain]], [[Italy]], [[Romania]], [[Germany]], [[Switzerland]], the [[Czech Republic]], and [[European Russia]]).<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://apps.kew.org/wcsp/namedetail.do?name_id=287247|title=World Checklist of Selected Plant Families: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew|website=apps.kew.org|language=en-GB|access-date=2017-01-30}}</ref> In Mexico, it is reported from [[Campeche]], [[Nayarit]], [[Tabasco]], [[Tamaulipas]], [[Puebla]], [[Jalisco]], [[Durango]], [[Tlaxcala]], [[Estado de México]], [[Veracruz]] and [[Michoacán]].<ref>Zepeda Gómez, Carmen, Lot, Antonio. Distribución y uso tradicional de ''Sagittaria macrophylla'' Zucc. y ''S. latifolia'' Willd. en el Estado de MéxicoCiencia Ergo Sum [online] 2005, 12</ref>

It can be found in wet areas such as ponds and swamps.<ref name="Audubon2001" />

==Ecology==
Extremely frequent as an [[emergent plant]], broadleaf arrowhead forms dense colonies on very wet [[soil]]s that become more open as the species mixes with other species of deeper water levels. These colonies form long bands following the curves of [[river]]s, [[pond]]s and [[lake]]s, well-marked by the dark green color of the leaves. The plant has strong roots and can survive through wide [[Statistical dispersion|variation]]s of the water level, slow [[current (stream)|current]]s and [[wave]]s. It displays an [[Chemical affinity|affinity]] for high levels of [[phosphate]]s and [[hard water]]s.

Despite the name "duck potato", [[duck]]s rarely consume the tubers, which are usually buried too deep for them to reach, although they often eat the [[seed]]s. [[Beaver]]s, [[North American porcupine]]s, and [[muskrat]]s eat the whole plant, tubers included. Native Americans are alleged to have opened muskrat houses to obtain their collection of roots.<ref name=Audubon>{{cite book |last1=Niering |first1=William A. |author-link1=William Niering| last2=Olmstead |first2=Nancy C. |title=The Audubon Society Field Guide to North American Wildflowers, Eastern Region |year=1985 |orig-date=1979|publisher=Knopf |isbn=0-394-50432-1 |page=318}}</ref>

This plant is vulnerable to aphids and spider mites.{{Citation needed|date=May 2021}}

==Cultivation==
This plant is easily cultivated in {{Convert|0.15|to|0.45|m|abbr=on|frac=2|in}} of water with no or little current. The tubers are planted well spaced (no more than 12 plants per square meter) at the end of May at a depth of {{Convert|5|to|7|cm|abbr=on|frac=2|in}}. [[Fertilize]] with decomposed [[manure]]. They can be multiplied through [[seed]]ing or division in July. The starchy tubers, produced by rhizomes beneath the wet ground surface, have long been an important food source to the [[indigenous peoples of the Americas]], along with those of ''S. cuneata''.<ref name=Audubon/> The tubers can be detached from the ground in various ways: with the feet, a [[pitchfork]], or a stick, and after digging up, the tubers usually float to the surface. Ripe tubers can be collected in the autumn, and are also often found then floating freely.<ref>{{cite web | url = http://www.ipni.org/ipni/plantNameByVersion.do?id=58518-1&version=1.1.2.1&show_history=true&back_page=%2Fipni%2FeditSimplePlantNameSearch.do%3Ffind_wholeName%3DSagittaria%2Blatifolia%26output_format%3Dnormal | title = 58518-1 | access-date = 2007-07-21 | date = 2004-07-14 | publisher = IPNI | quote = Alismataceae Sagittaria latifolia Willd. Sp. Pl. iv. 409.}}</ref>

== Uses ==
The starchy tubers were consumed by Native Americans<ref name="Audubon2001" /> in the lower [[Columbia River]] basin,<ref name="Freedman1976">{{cite journal |last=Freedman |first=Robert Louis |date=1976 |title=Native North American Food Preparation Techniques |journal=Boletín Bibliográfico de Antropología Americana (1973-1979) |language=en |publisher=Pan American Institute of Geography and History |volume=38 |issue=47 |page=127 |jstor=43996285}}, s.v. Swamp Potato (''wappato'') Oregon</ref><ref name="Wildflowers" /> in addition to the [[Omaha people|Omaha]]<ref name="BRIT-Omaha">{{cite web |title=Native American Ethnobotany Database |url=http://naeb.brit.org/uses/35595/ |access-date=2021-12-09 |website=[[Botanical Research Institute of Texas]]}}</ref> and [[Cherokee]] nations.<ref name="Freedman1976" /> The tubers can be eaten raw or cooked for 15 to 20 minutes. The taste is similar to [[potato]]es and [[chestnut]]s, and they can be prepared in the same fashions: [[roasting]], [[frying]], [[boiling]], and so on. They can also be [[cutting|slice]]d and [[Drying (food)|dried]] to prepare a [[flour]].<ref>{{cite web | url = http://www.pfaf.org/database/plants.php?Sagittaria+latifolia | title = ''Sagittaria latifolia'' - Willd. Duck Potato | access-date = 2007-07-20 |date= June 2004 | work = Edible and medicinal plant database | publisher = Plants For A Future | quote = Excellent when roasted, the texture is somewhat like potatoes with a taste like sweet chestnuts }}</ref>

Other edible parts include late summer [[bud]]s and [[fruit]]s.{{Citation needed|date=May 2021}}

==Culture==
The name of [[Shubenacadie, Nova Scotia|Shubenacadie]], a community located in central [[Nova Scotia]], [[Canada]], means "abounding in ground nuts" (i.e., broadleaf arrowhead) in the [[Mi'kmaq language]].{{Citation needed|date=May 2021}}
